card.title: Valence Shell, Valence Electron and Octet Theory

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Bonding exists to copy noble-gas stability. The **valence shell** (outermost shell) supplies the electrons; the **octet rule** of Kossel and Lewis says atoms reach ns²np⁶ either by transferring electrons (Kossel — ionic bonds, NaCl, MgO) or sharing pairs (Lewis — covalent bonds, Cl₂, CH₄), while hydrogen and lithium settle for the helium duet.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Valence electrons = group number (main-group elements) - Valency (non-metals) = 8 − valence electrons - Total valence e⁻ = Σ valence e⁻ (atoms) ± charge (anion +, cation −)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Octet counts electrons, not bonds:** CO₂'s carbon has 8 electrons but only 2 bonds (double bonds count four electrons each).  ·  **Valency vs valence electrons:** for non-metals valency = 8 − valence electrons (Cl: 7 valence e⁻, valency 1).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***SF₆ holds 12 electrons around sulphur*** — an expanded octet possible only from period 3, where 3d orbitals are energetically accessible.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The octet rule is a stability statement, not a shape theory — it decides how many electrons gather around an atom; VSEPR decides where they point. Electron-deficient species (BF₃) are Lewis acids precisely because their octets are short.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Valence shell = outermost shell; its electrons do the bonding. Octet rule (Kossel–Lewis 1916): eight electrons in the outer shell via transfer (ionic) or sharing (covalent); duet for H/Li.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Helium completes its shell with just two electrons — the duet — because n = 1 holds only 1s²; it is the only noble gas whose "octet" is a pair.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Atoms Bother to Bond Every bond answers one question: how does an atom reach the **stability of a noble gas**? Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar…) are chemically inert because their valence shells are complete — ns²np⁶, an **octet** (or the duet of helium). All other atoms borrow, give, or share electrons to copy that arrangement.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Valence shell and valence electrons - **Valence shell:** the outermost occupied shell of an atom (highest n). **Valence electrons:** the electrons in it — the only electrons that participate in bonding. - Examples: Na (2,8,1) has 1 valence electron; Cl (2,8,7) has 7; C (2,4) has 4. Core electrons stay spectators.…  ·  ## 3. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 How the rule generates formulae - Na (2,8,1) transfers one electron to Cl (2,8,7): both reach (2,8) and (2,8,8) — **Na⁺Cl⁻**, formula NaCl. - Mg (2,8,2) gives one electron each to two Cl atoms → **MgCl₂**; Mg gives two to O → **MgO**.…  ·  ### Deep dive — octet theory: the rule, its basis and its exceptions Kossel and Lewis (1916) explained bonding by the drive toward a noble-gas valence shell (ns²np⁶, eight electrons). Atoms achieve it by **transfer** (ionic), **sharing** (covalent) or **donation of a pair** (coordinate).…

Common Confusions **Octet ≠ eight bonds:** the octet counts electrons *around* an atom (bonding pairs counted twice, once per atom), not bonds. In CO₂ carbon owns 8 electrons via two double bonds — but forms only two bonds.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Valence electrons vs valency:** Cl has 7 valence electrons but valency 1 — valency is 8 − valence electrons (for non-metals), not the count itself.  ·  **Expanded octets are third-row-only:** C, N, O, F (period 2) have no accessible d orbitals; P, S, Cl and beyond can exceed 8. Never write five bonds on carbon.  ·  ## 7.
